items.label: Main aim
items.prompt: Find the sentence that states the MAIN aim of the study.
items.model: To explore how sleep relates to students' academic performance by objectively tracking their sleep with Fitbits for a whole semester.
items.why: 'Our aim in this study was…' states the primary aim; it is repeated more specifically a few sentences later.

items.label: Secondary aim
items.model: To understand gender differences in sleep and academic performance.
items.why: Articles can have more than one aim; 'A secondary aim was…' introduces it.

items.label: Hypothesis
items.prompt: Does the article state a formal hypothesis?
options: Yes, that better sleep will predict better grades
No, it states aims but no formal hypothesis
Yes, but only about gender differences
items.ans: No, it states aims but no formal hypothesis
items.model: No: the Introduction states aims ('we aimed to relate…', 'we aim to see whether…') but no prediction.
items.why: 'We aim to see whether' is an aim, not a prediction.

items.label: Variables
items.prompt: Name the three sleep measures (predictors) and the outcome variable.
items.model: Predictors: sleep duration, sleep quality, sleep (in)consistency. Outcome: overall score (quizzes + midterms).
items.why: These three regressors were entered into the regression on overall score.

items.label: Conceptual definition
items.prompt: Find the CONCEPTUAL definition of sleep inconsistency in the Introduction.
items.model: Inconsistency in sleep schedule and/or duration from day to day ('social jet lag').
items.why: '…is defined by…' in the Introduction explains what the concept means.

items.label: Operational definition
items.prompt: Now find the OPERATIONAL definition of sleep inconsistency (how it was calculated).
items.model: The standard deviation of each participant's daily sleep duration; a larger SD = more inconsistency.
items.why: Compare with the conceptual definition: this one tells you the exact calculation, and it appears in the Results, not the Methods.

items.label: Operational definition (quality)
items.model: Fitbit's proprietary algorithm, giving a score from 0 (poor) to 10 (good).
items.why: This journal places the Methods AFTER the Discussion, so look at the end of the article.

items.label: Theoretical explanation
items.prompt: There's no section called 'theoretical framework'. Find the sentence that introduces the main theoretical idea linking sleep to learning.
items.model: Sleep plays a crucial role in memory consolidation: active synaptic connections are strengthened during sleep.
items.why: The framework is the memory consolidation account, introduced without being labelled.

items.label: Research gap
items.prompt: Find the sentence in the INTRODUCTION that states the research gap.
items.model: Previous studies used subjective self-report measures of sleep; very few used objective measures.
items.why: 'Although numerous studies… very few to date have…' signals the gap.

items.label: General method
items.prompt: What general method did this study use?
items.model: Correlational: sleep was observed, not manipulated.
items.why: The authors note that establishing cause would require randomised experiments, which they did not run.

items.label: Final sample
items.prompt: Find the sentence giving the number of participants who COMPLETED the study.
items.model: 88 participants completed the study (45 female; mostly freshmen; mean age 18.19).
items.why: 100 volunteers were selected, but 12 were excluded; the final sample was 88.

items.label: Exclusions
items.prompt: Find the sentence explaining why participants were EXCLUDED.
items.model: 7 wore the tracker <80% of the semester, 3 lost it, 2 completed <75% of assessments.
items.why: Exclusion reasons explain the difference between the recruited and final sample.

items.label: Night-before finding
items.prompt: Was sleep on the NIGHT BEFORE a midterm related to the midterm score?
items.why: Read the 'Night before assessments' results; all p values were above .05.

items.label: Variance explained
items.prompt: What percentage of the variance in overall score did the three sleep measures explain together?
items.why: R² tells you how much variance the predictors explain together.

items.label: Ruling out an alternative explanation
items.prompt: Some participants were also in an intense exercise class. Find the sentence explaining why they were still included.
items.model: They didn't differ from other participants in grade, exercise, sleep amount or sleep quality.
items.why: Checking that a subgroup doesn't differ is one way to rule out an alternative explanation.

items.label: Overclaiming
items.prompt: In the Discussion, find a sentence that uses CAUSAL wording even though the study is correlational.
items.model: '…better content-relevant sleep LEADS TO improved performance…'
items.why: 'Leads to' implies cause, which a correlational design can't show. The authors themselves admit this in the limitations.

items.label: Practical implication
items.prompt: Find the sentence stating what the timing findings imply for students.
items.model: Sleep matters most while content is being learned; just sleeping well the night before may not help much.
items.why: 'The implications of these findings are…' signals an implication.

items.label: Limitation (measurement)
items.prompt: Find the limitation about the VALIDITY of the sleep quality measure.
items.model: No published evidence that Fitbit's 1–10 sleep quality score is a valid measure of sleep quality.
items.why: This links to validity: does the measure actually measure what it claims?

items.label: Limitation (generalisability)
items.model: One course of MIT students; future studies need other populations and classes.
items.why: The Third limitation is about who the findings apply to.
